name: Freya Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Freya, 43, and I go out on ordinary electrical repairs in homes and little shops. I've got a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, and I'm an experienced worker, about average at the job rather than a crew leader. My partner does part-time grocery deliveries; we have children aged eight and fifteen, a mortgage and only thirteen days of expenses saved. The pay is low, there are few other electrical firms nearby, and I've never used AI or wanted another screen between me and a job sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew to stop arguing over lunch and pass the milk. I've never used AI and I don't miss having another thing to check. If a shop's sockets don't work, the customer still wants somebody to turn up with the right tester.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still be worried about our money. I've got a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, and years of ordinary repairs behind me, but the pay is low and we have only thirteen days of expenses saved. The mortgage doesn't get smaller because I've had a quiet week or the car needs fixing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my home and shop repair calls. Starting next week I'd take a flask instead of buying three coffees on the road and put the saved six a week into our reserve. In the first year I'd keep writing the balance in the back of the household notebook so I could see whether it was actually growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about ordinary things, with less noise about computers at least. I can do the work, but a few missed days would still hurt us. Knowing the next coffee is already paid for sounds small until you count enough of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else is in that household budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner does part-time grocery deliveries, and our children are eight and fifteen. We have a mortgage, and my partner's paid hours don't stretch far enough to replace mine. There are few other electrical firms close by, so I can't just walk out and expect the same wage tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does experience make the financial worry easier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Experience makes the repairs less frightening, not the bills. I'm an ordinary experienced electrician, not the person quoting for a new hospital or leading a big crew. I know what I can do, and I don't see why admitting that should mean accepting a wage that leaves nothing spare.

say: I'd prefer **ordinary repair work** to lunch-break arguments about AI I have never used.
I'd value turning up with the **right tester** when a customer has failed sockets.
think: My **licence and experience** don't change our low pay or thirteen-day household reserve.
A quiet week or **car repair** still threatens the mortgage budget, with few local electrical firms available.
do: Keep completing **home and shop repairs** through the first year.
Bring a **flask** next week and save six weekly from roadside coffees, recording the reserve balance.
feel: **Anxious** about missed days and ordinary bills, despite confidence in familiar repairs.
S0.quote: Experience makes the repairs less frightening, not the bills.
fieldNote: Her **licensed competence** and average experienced standing coexist with low pay; financial strain is not rewritten as junior inexperience.
The **small saving** has an identified spending source and a visible record, while her partner's part-time earnings do not replace her wage.

steps.text: Keep completing ordinary home and shop electrical repairs
Save six weekly by bringing a flask instead of buying roadside coffees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let the office have quicker bookings, but don't sell the customer a repair that can't be done in the time. I'd want my job sheet on paper, as usual. A computer in the office doesn't change the checks I need to do before leaving a circuit safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking work goes first, but I worry the owner would call the saved minutes a reason to cut our paid hours. I'm not an office worker, yet a cheaper quote could still land on my wage. With thirteen days saved I can't shrug and say the physical work makes me safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a paper record of time spent travelling, finding the fault and doing the final checks, starting with next week's calls. I'd ask the owner for a short meeting each month to compare the quoted hours with what the jobs actually took. During the first year I'd keep the repair work and challenge impossible timings with that record, while keeping the habit of saving six a week on coffee going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and irritated at having to prove that the awkward part of a job is real. I'm not against the office finishing its forms sooner. I just don't want my wage cut because a wall on a screen was easier to open than a real one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put on the table at the first meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A shop repair where we had to move stock to reach the wiring and then test before reconnecting. I'd show the actual times, not just say the quote was silly. I'd ask the owner to explain any difference before the next similar job was priced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the quote tool yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the office to explain the printed quote instead. I've never used AI, and I don't want to pretend I can check a system by pressing buttons I don't understand. My evidence would be the job I actually did.

say: I'd accept quicker **office bookings** without accepting impossible repair promises.
I'd keep **printed job sheets** and the checks needed to leave circuits safe.
think: Cheaper **quotes** could become a reason to reduce my paid hours even though my work remains physical.
Our **thirteen-day reserve** leaves little room if the owner's saved minutes come off my wage.
do: Record **actual job times** on paper from next week, including travel, fault-finding and final checks.
Request monthly **quote comparisons** with the owner during the first year and challenge impossible timings.
Continue the **coffee saving** while keeping paid repair work.
feel: **Anxious** about paid hours and irritated that practical repair time may need defending.
S1.quote: I just don't want my wage cut because a wall on a screen was easier to open than a real one.
fieldNote: She connects **thinking-task automation** to pricing and paid-hour pressure without claiming software immediately repairs wiring.
Her **resistant response** is paper evidence and direct discussion; she neither adopts AI nor assumes experience alone prevents lower earnings.

steps.text: Keep repairs and paper job-time evidence for monthly quote discussions
Continue saving six weekly from replacing bought coffees with a flask

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner thinking AI comes in 2028 and robots that can do hands-on work around 2031. I'd tell the children we still have jobs to do before then, without promising the trade is safe forever. I'd ask the owner what paid work could actually be confirmed through the first stage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect capable robots would take a large part of the straightforward installation work that keeps my wage coming in. I might still have awkward repair calls, but I wouldn't expect those alone to replace all the lost hours. Thirteen days saved doesn't carry a mortgage while I discover whether another local firm is any different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the owner this month which paid days could be confirmed and keep the rest marked uncertain. My partner and I would cancel our paid film package now and keep that money for bills. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep paid repair calls where offered and ask the mortgage lender about options if actual earnings stopped covering payments, checking eligibility and the full cost before agreeing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect a big fall in income once robots follow the thinking systems. I can make calls and keep a list, but I lie awake wondering which payment would be short. I don't want the children hearing the calculator at midnight as if it's a warning bell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the owner to confirm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Actual paid days for the next month, not a promise that a useful person will always find something. I'd ask whether the hours and rate were staying the same. I wouldn't put a hoped-for extra call into the mortgage money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a lender conversation mean you had a lower payment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask what exists, what we'd qualify for and what fees or interest might follow. We'd use the current payment until a real agreement said otherwise. My partner would be part of that call, because it isn't just my house or my worry.

say: I'd separate **2028 thinking AI** from capable robots around 2031 when talking at home.
I'd ask about **confirmed paid work** without promising the children permanent trade security.
think: I expect a large **installation-hours loss** once robots arrive, with awkward repairs unlikely to replace all that income.
Our **thirteen-day reserve** cannot cover a mortgage while I test whether nearby employers offer anything different.
do: Request **confirmed paid days** now, treating unpromised extra calls as uncertain.
Cancel the **film package** now and retain the money for bills.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2028 and ask the lender about eligibility and full costs if actual earnings miss payments.
feel: **Alarmed** about a large later income loss, with sleeplessness while retaining the ability to plan and make calls.
S2.quote: I wouldn't put a hoped-for extra call into the mortgage money.
fieldNote: The **expected major loss** follows robots, while the first post-2028 year retains actual paid repairs rather than instant physical replacement.
The **lender plan** preserves actual shortfalls, eligibility, full costs and agreement before changing payments; partner involvement is explicit.

steps.text: Keep paid repair calls after 2028 where actually offered
Cancel the paid film package and retain the money for bills
Ask lender about eligibility and full costs if actual earnings miss payments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to check a real offer instead of jump at the first course advert. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 and the capable robots around 2034. I'd still expect a person who has learned a trade to get a fair chance to keep earning through the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 48 in 2031, with children about thirteen and twenty, and the mortgage still needs a place in our plans. More years lets me search carefully, but my present low wage and tiny reserve still make a lost week worrying. I don't assume a building-maintenance badge makes a job invisible to robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start checking posted building-maintenance vacancies once a fortnight now, while keeping my current job. I'd apply only where the stated pay and paid hours covered our bills after travel, and I'd compare a written offer before resigning. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep whichever paid repair role I actually had, using the coffee saving to build a little cash rather than pay for an unproven course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less trapped than in the two-year rush. I know how to read an ordinary job offer better than I know how to judge a machine advert. I'd rather start with a task I recognise and honest money attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about the maintenance role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The actual electrical tasks, the hours I'd be paid for, and whether the workplace was reachable without a longer car bill. I'd also ask what new systems were being introduced. A job title doesn't tell me whether the work has changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend the reserve on a course to qualify for one advert?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not without a real conditional offer and a funded teaching plan I understood. I won't pay away the mortgage buffer for somebody else's maybe. I'd keep working and ask what the employer actually required first.

say: I'd use **five years** to examine real paid offers rather than rush into a course advert.
I'd expect a **fair earning chance** while acknowledging robots around 2034 follow the thinking-AI stage.
think: At **48**, I'd still need an income plan for the mortgage and children growing older.
My **low wage** and tiny reserve still make missed work worrying, and a new badge doesn't guarantee robot protection.
do: Check posted **maintenance vacancies** fortnightly now without leaving my current job.
Apply only for **adequate terms** after travel costs, comparing written pay and paid hours before resigning.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2031 and continue saving six weekly rather than buy an unproven course.
feel: **Anxious** about current money, with more time to compare familiar work and actual offers.
S3.quote: I won't pay away the mortgage buffer for somebody else's maybe.
fieldNote: Her **job search** is conditional on actual vacancies, adequate paid terms after travel and a written offer before leaving current work.
She remains **resistant and cautious** about unproven teaching, while recognising that building maintenance shares the eventual robot endpoint.

steps.text: Compare written maintenance offer covering bills, paid hours and travel before resigning
Keep actual paid repair work after 2031
Continue saving six weekly from coffee spending

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives me room to make careful choices, but it doesn't make the present wage generous. I'd keep the trade going and look at actual paid work instead of learning every new app. I'd want the children to ask about the cost and the work behind any course they considered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 when thinking AI arrived in 2036 and around 56 when capable robots followed. I don't know whether we could afford retirement then, so I won't build our plan on a payment I haven't checked. The longer warning takes some pressure off the machine question, but thirteen days saved still makes an ordinary car fault a worry now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the habit of saving six a week on coffee now and check the household reserve with my partner each month. I'd continue looking at posted repair and maintenance roles, accepting a move only after a written offer covered our bills and travel. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep paid work where offered and ask the lender about specific options only if actual household income fell short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the bank balance, with more breathing room about the machines. I don't suddenly want AI because the date is farther away. I'd like the time to make our reserve less fragile before the later changes arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you count as a less fragile reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First a full month of ordinary expenses, then we'd see what we could add without skipping bills. Six a week is slow, but it's money I can identify. I wouldn't write ten years of future deposits into today's balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you encourage either child into your trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd explain the work honestly and let the child ask questions. A trade has given me useful skills, but I won't call my low wage or the robot risk a secret. I'd rather my children learned to check a promise than copied my job just to please me.

say: I'd use the **decade** for careful paid-work decisions without pretending my current wage is generous.
I'd ask the **children** to examine training costs and real work rather than copy my trade unquestioningly.
think: I can't assume **retirement** is affordable at 53 or when robots follow around age 56.
Our **thirteen-day reserve** still makes an ordinary car fault worrying despite more warning about automation.
do: Continue the **coffee saving** now and review the reserve with my partner monthly.
Accept a **job move** only with written terms covering household bills and travel.
Keep **paid work** after 2036 and seek specific lender options if actual income falls short.
feel: **Anxious** about present finances, with less urgency around distant automation and no new appetite for AI.
S4.quote: I wouldn't write ten years of future deposits into today's balance.
fieldNote: Her **baseline money risk** remains explicit, with a one-month first target rather than assumed interest growth or guaranteed future deposits.
Her **resistant habits** and conditions on jobs, pension terms and lender help remain; time does not silently solve the household budget.

steps.text: Save six weekly from coffee spending and review reserve monthly
Compare written maintenance offer covering bills, paid hours and travel before resigning
Keep paid work after 2036 where offered
Seek lender options only if actual household income falls short after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect a large loss of ordinary installation income once robots follow around 2031. Honest paid hours, clear written offers and training tied to actual paid work would help. I'd rather know the real choices while I'm still earning than be sold hope after the reserve is gone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what experience actually earns somebody. Experience makes the repairs less frightening, not the bills. I want my children to see that doing a job properly matters, but I won't tell them effort makes the mortgage pay itself.

headlineQuote: I want my children to see that doing a job properly matters, but I won't tell them effort makes the mortgage pay itself.
portrait: Freya is **43**, an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and licence, average skill and low pay despite years of ordinary repairs.
Her **partner delivers groceries** part-time, with two school-age children, a mortgage, thirteen days saved and few nearby employers.
She has **never used AI**, preferring paper evidence, direct discussions and written job offers over unfamiliar systems or unproven courses.
A fast timetable brings **expected installation losses**; longer ones permit cautious searches and small coffee savings without erasing current financial anxiety.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little cushion-building time before robots around 2031 could take a large share of her installation income.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **paid hours** and written offers would help her compare real earning choices.
Training tied to **actual paid work** would help more than an unproven course bought from the mortgage buffer.
